For in this way, the one who is higher than all of these is presented, and it is correct that the focus is not on the superiority of each individual element. Why so? Because there is no purpose in doing so. No purpose is seen or heard of in the scriptures regarding the individual superiority of the other elements <note>such as the senses and mind</note>. However, regarding the <term>Purusha</term> <gloss>the Supreme Person or Consciousness</gloss>, who is higher than the senses and the rest, and who transcends the entire realm of objects, a purpose is seen: the attainment of <term>Moksha</term> <gloss>liberation</gloss>. Thus says the <term>Shruti</term> <gloss>scripture</gloss>: Having perceived That, one is released from the jaws of death <note>Katha Upanishad 3.15</note>. Moreover, by denying anything higher than the <term>Purusha</term> and by using the word <term>Kastha</term> <gloss>the ultimate goal/pinnacle</gloss>, the scripture shows its primary regard for the <term>Purusha</term>. It shows that the progression of preceding and succeeding elements is for the sake of realizing the <term>Purusha</term>. As for the phrase for the sake of the story: it means for the sake of right knowledge which is preceded by the story. This story is taught only for the purpose of right knowledge, and the story itself is not the primary objective.

**And because of the word Atman. (15)**

For this reason also, the description of the sequence of the senses and so on is intended only for the realization of the <term>Purusha</term>. The reason is that the scripture refers to the <term>Purusha</term> under discussion as the <term>Atman</term> <gloss>the Self</gloss>, saying: This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; but it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect <note>Katha Upanishad 3.12</note>. From this, it is understood that the others <note>senses, objects, mind</note> are not intended to be regarded as the Self. It also shows the difficulty of knowing Him and that He is attainable by a refined intellect. For the very purpose of knowing Him, the scripture prescribes the method: The wise man should restrain speech in the mind <note>Katha Upanishad 3.13</note>. This was already explained under the section Beginning with the Inference <note>Brahma Sutra 1.4.1</note>. Thus, in various ways...

->**Bhamati**<-

Furthermore, the Veda, by the sign of denying anything beyond <note>There is nothing beyond the Purusha</note> and by the sign of the <term>Purusha</term> being the goal of all things, shows that the intent is on the <term>Purusha</term>. It shows that the mention of the superiority of one element over another is for that purpose; this is stated in the phrase moreover. Because objects and the rest have no independent purpose, the author connects the sutra by saying for the sake of the story, meaning for the sake of the vision of the <term>Purusha</term> preceded by those superiorities. **And because of the word Atman.** Since there is a consistency between the beginning and the end in phrases like That is the supreme step of Vishnu and There is nothing higher than the Purusha, it is certain that the whole passage forms a single sentence focused on the one <term>Purusha</term>. Therefore, it is not proper to imagine a split in the sentence or a split in the results, as that would be unnecessarily complex.

->**Nyaya Nirnaya**<-

To the question "Why?", the author replies "Because of the lack of purpose," thinking that since there is no result from knowing the superiority of the senses and so on, it cannot be the intended meaning. To the doubt that there might be a purpose, he denies it by saying "No." To the second alternative <note>that a result is heard in scripture</note>, he says "nor is it heard." Since this context is seen to concern the nature of reality and not injunctions for meditation, and since it is possible for it to concern the knowledge of the Supreme Goal, it is not proper to assume it concerns the superiority of individual senses. One might object that the knowledge of the <term>Purusha's</term> superiority is also not fruitful. He replies "But in the <term>Purusha</term>," stating that the vision of the <term>Purusha</term> as higher than the senses—characterized by the absence of objects and being unconditioned—is experienced as the destruction of ignorance. He says "It is seen," meaning the removal of ignorance and false knowledge is a visible result. For those who disagree with the experience of the wise, he cites the <term>Shruti</term>: "Thus." He adds "Moreover" to show this is the total intent of the context. The Veda shows its regard for the <term>Purusha</term> by the word <term>Kastha</term> <gloss>pinnacle</gloss>. The "progression" refers to the superiority of each succeeding element over the preceding one. He explains the part of the sutra "for the sake of the story" to counter the idea that it refers to an injunction for meditation. **And because of the word Atman.** He explains the "and" in the sutra with "For this reason." He clarifies the word <term>Atman</term> by saying "Which." He removes the doubt that the non-manifestation of the Self is natural by saying "But it is seen." He shows that the difficulty of knowing the Self is due to the excellence of the intent regarding the beginning and end of the text.

<summary>Shankara argues that the hierarchical progression of the senses and mind in the Katha Upanishad is not to teach their individual importance, but to guide the seeker toward the Supreme Purusha (Self), which is the only source of liberation.</summary>
<keywords>Adi Shankara, Brahma Sutras, Katha Upanishad, Purusha, Atman, Moksha, Bhamati, Nyaya Nirnaya, hierarchy of being, liberation</keywords>
